learn.title: Direct Air Capture: Removing CO2 with Renewables
learn.intro: Direct Air Capture (DAC) pulls CO2 straight from the atmosphere using renewable energy, offering a way to reverse emissions even from sectors hard to electrify. With global DAC capacity under 0.1 Mt annually, scaling this technology could remove billions of tons of CO2 yearly, playing a key role in net-zero goals.
learn.c1_text: India emits over 2.6 billion tons of CO2 annually, making it the world’s third-largest emitter. While DAC isn’t yet deployed at scale here, integrating it with India’s growing renewable base—like its 90 GW solar capacity—could support long-term net-zero targets. Pilot projects may emerge under green hydrogen missions.
learn.c2_text: DAC requires 1,000–2,000 kWh per ton of CO2 captured, making cheap renewables essential. Solar and wind can power these systems when generation is high. Pairing DAC with excess renewable energy turns curtailment into carbon removal—an elegant solution for balancing grids and cleaning the atmosphere.
learn.stat3: Energy needed: 1,000–2,000 kWh per ton CO2

learn.title: Solid-State Batteries: Safer, Denser Energy Storage
learn.intro: Solid-state batteries replace liquid electrolytes with solids, boosting safety and energy density—crucial for electric vehicles and grid storage. Unlike today’s lithium-ion packs, they reduce fire risks and charge faster. As India pushes EV adoption, this tech could redefine mobility and renewable integration.
learn.c1_text: Imagine swapping a water balloon for a sponge—solid-state batteries do just that by replacing flammable liquids with ceramics or polymers. This change prevents fires and allows thinner layers, packing 2–3x more energy. A typical EV battery might go from 300 miles to over 600 miles per charge.
learn.c2_text: The solid electrolyte must conduct ions efficiently while resisting dendrites—metal spikes that short circuits. Materials like sulfides and oxides show promise. Companies aim for 2030 mass production. These advances could slash battery costs and boost lifespans, vital for India’s goal of 30% EV sales by 2030.
learn.c3_text: India plans to localize 70% of EV supply chains by 2030 under its National Mission on Interdisciplinary Cyber-Physical Systems. With FAME scheme incentives and Gigafactories coming up, solid-state R&D partnerships with global firms could position India as a future battery hub. IIT Madras is already testing indigenous prototypes.
learn.stat3: Fire risk reduced by replacing liquid electrolyte
learn.stat4: India to localize 70% of EV supply chain by 2030

learn.title: Demand Response: Smart Energy Use for Grid Stability
learn.intro: Demand response lets large electricity users reduce usage during peak times in exchange for payments, helping balance supply and demand without building new power plants. It’s a smart, low-cost tool that supports renewables and lowers grid strain—especially critical as India adds record solar capacity.
learn.c1_text: Think of demand response like adjusting your schedule during rush hour—it eases congestion. When the grid is stressed, factories or malls dim lights or pause operations briefly. In return, they get paid. California saved 2,700 MW in 2022—enough for 2 million homes—through such programs.
learn.c2_text: Smart thermostats and industrial controllers receive real-time price signals or grid alerts. They automatically adjust loads to match supply. For example, refrigerators can pre-cool before peak pricing hits. This flexibility stabilizes voltage and frequency, enabling deeper renewable penetration without compromising reliability.
learn.c3_text: India launched its National Demand Response Program to manage peak demand, which often exceeds 200 GW. States like Gujarat and Maharashtra pilot demand-side management with industries. As renewable share grows, DR will be key to managing variability—especially with solar peaking at noon when demand dips.
learn.stat1: California saved 2,700 MW via DR in 2022
learn.stat3: Solar peaks at noon, lowest demand period
learn.stat4: India launched National Demand Response Program

learn.title: Building Integrated Photovoltaics: Solar as Architecture
learn.intro: Building Integrated Photovoltaics (BIPV) embed solar cells into building materials—rooftops, facades, windows—turning structures into power generators. Unlike traditional panels, BIPV replaces conventional materials, saving space and enhancing aesthetics. India’s urban growth makes BIPV ideal for sustainable cities.
learn.c1_text: BIPV works like wearing a jacket that also charges your phone—every surface becomes functional. Solar tiles replace roofing shingles; tinted PV glass serves as windows. A 10-story office building with BIPV facade can generate 1 MW annually, offsetting 1 million kg of CO2 each year.
learn.c2_text: Modern BIPV modules offer varying transparency levels, allowing daylight control while generating power. Thin-film technologies like CIGS are flexible and lightweight, suitable for curved surfaces. Architects now design net-positive buildings that produce more energy than they consume—an exciting frontier in green construction.
learn.c3_text: India’s Smart Cities Mission promotes energy-efficient infrastructure. BIPV fits perfectly—Delhi’s Indira Gandhi International Airport uses rooftop solar extensively. Startups like Tata Power Solar are developing BIPV solutions tailored for tropical climates. Policy push through RPOs could accelerate deployment in metro areas.

learn.stat2: Offsets 1 million kg CO2/year per building
learn.stat3: India has 100+ smart cities under development

learn.title: Agrivoltaics: Solar Panels Meet Farming
learn.intro: Agrivoltaics combines solar farms with agriculture on the same land, maximizing land use efficiency. Crops grow beneath elevated panels, benefiting from shade and reduced evaporation. This dual-use approach boosts both food and energy output—ideal for densely populated countries like India facing land scarcity.
learn.c1_text: Picture a tennis court split between solar panels and lettuce beds—both thrive together. Elevated panels cast light shade, reducing heat stress on plants. Studies show agrivoltaic systems increase crop yields by 30–100% while maintaining solar efficiency. Water savings reach up to 20% due to lower evaporation.
learn.c2_text: Panel height and spacing are tuned to crop needs. Tomatoes grow well under partial shade, while leafy greens prefer full sun. Sensors monitor soil moisture and light levels. Some setups use tracking panels to follow the sun, optimizing both photosyntheses and energy capture—an elegant synergy of nature and tech.
learn.c3_text: India has over 1.5 million sq km of cultivable waste land—prime for agrivoltaics. Research at IIT Bombay explores suitable crops like fenugreek and spinach under solar canopies. With 90 GW solar installed and rising, this model supports farmer income and climate resilience. MNRE may soon include agrivoltaics in solar park guidelines.
learn.stat1: India has 1.5 million sq km of cultivable waste land
learn.stat3: Water savings up to 20% due to reduced evaporation

learn.title: Green Ammonia: Clean Fuel for Shipping and Fertilizers
learn.intro: Green ammonia is made using hydrogen from water split by renewable energy and nitrogen from air—no fossil fuels involved. It stores clean energy and powers ships, trucks, and fertilizers without carbon emissions. As India plans 500 GW renewables by 2030, green ammonia offers a path to decarbonize heavy transport and agriculture.
learn.c1_text: Green ammonia acts like a battery in liquid form—storing summer solar power for winter use. Made via electrolysis and Haber-Bosch process using wind/solar, it carries ~17.6% hydrogen by weight. Japan imports it as fuel; ships burn it directly. One ton offsets 3 tons of CO2 compared to coal-based ammonia.
learn.c2_text: Producing green ammonia needs 9–12 MWh per ton—costly today but falling fast. Electrolyzers and renewable electricity dominate expenses. Ports must retrofit engines and safety gear. Still, long-haul shipping emits 3% of global CO2. Switching to green ammonia could cut maritime emissions dramatically by 2050.
learn.c3_text: India aims to become a top green ammonia exporter by 2030. NTPC and IOCL are building pilot plants. Gujarat and Rajasthan offer ideal conditions for solar-powered ammonia. Under the National Green Hydrogen Mission, India targets 5 MTY of green hydrogen/ammonia capacity. Export corridors to Japan and EU are being explored.
learn.stat1: Green ammonia stores 17.6% hydrogen by weight
learn.stat2: Requires 9–12 MWh per ton to produce
learn.stat3: India targets 5 MTY green hydrogen/ammonia by 2030
